prompt:
A 67-year-old man presents with two weeks of progressive painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, and a 4 kg unintentional weight loss. Examination reveals scleral icterus and a palpable, nontender gallbladder. Laboratory studies show a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a cholestatic pattern. What is the appropriate evaluation of this painless obstructive jaundice?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Obtain cross-sectional imaging with a pancreatic-protocol CT or MRI/MRCP to evaluate for pancreatic or biliary malignancy.
Obtain a right upper quadrant ultrasound to assess biliary dilation if definitive cross-sectional imaging has not already been obtained, without delaying pancreatic-protocol CT or MRI/MRCP.
Obtain a complete liver profile, including fractionated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, aminotransferases, and albumin.
Obtain a complete blood count and renal function testing as part of the initial evaluation.
Measure CA 19-9 as an adjunct tumor marker once the obstruction is being evaluated.
Refer urgently to gastroenterology and hepatobiliary surgery through a suspected malignancy pathway.
Perform endoscopic ultrasound with tissue sampling when histologic confirmation is required.

Perform ERCP with biliary stenting for noncholangitic malignant obstruction when drainage is indicated for palliation, severe refractory pruritus, planned neoadjuvant therapy, or a substantial delay to definitive surgery.
Assess promptly for cholangitis using symptoms, vital signs, examination, and laboratory findings.
Administer prompt intravenous antibiotics if cholangitis is diagnosed.
Obtain urgent biliary drainage if cholangitis is present.
Review the full medication and supplement list for potential hepatotoxins.
Check PT/INR to assess coagulopathy and possible vitamin K deficiency in the setting of cholestasis.
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when fever or other signs of cholangitis are present.
Obtain appropriate staging imaging, including chest imaging, if a malignancy is identified.
Review confirmed or strongly suspected malignancy in a multidisciplinary hepatopancreatobiliary team to determine resectability and treatment sequencing.
Proceed with surgical evaluation without requiring preoperative tissue confirmation when imaging shows a clearly resectable pancreatic malignancy.
Treat significant pruritus symptomatically while the obstructive cause is investigated.
Arrange expedited follow-up to review imaging, pathology, staging, and the definitive treatment plan.
Recheck bilirubin and cholestatic liver tests after biliary decompression to document response.
Attribute the jaundice to benign gallstones and discharge the patient without imaging.
Start ursodeoxycholic acid empirically without determining the cause of the obstruction.
Treat pruritus alone and defer evaluation of the obstruction.
Order hepatitis serologies alone and forgo cross-sectional imaging.
Use diagnostic ERCP as the first investigation before obtaining noninvasive cross-sectional imaging in a stable patient.
Place a routine preoperative biliary stent when prompt surgery is feasible and there is no cholangitis or other drainage indication.
Delay specialist referral while observing whether the jaundice resolves spontaneously.
Use a normal CA 19-9 result to exclude pancreatic or biliary malignancy.
Give empiric antibiotics in the absence of clinical evidence of cholangitis or another infection.
Start corticosteroids for presumed autoimmune pancreatitis without supportive imaging or diagnostic evaluation.
Perform cholecystectomy for presumed gallstone disease without first localizing the obstruction.
Perform percutaneous biopsy of a potentially resectable pancreatic mass before multidisciplinary review when endoscopic ultrasound sampling is available.
Withhold urgent biliary drainage despite established cholangitis.
Proceed directly to surgical exploration for suspected malignancy without staging or assessment of resectability.
